items.title: West Virginia Official Accused of Stealing 9 Properties for Friend With Ties to His Used Car Dealership
items.summary:
A West Virginia state auditor has been indicted for his role in an alleged scheme to steal nine properties from their owners and sell them to benefit a longtime friend and business associate—who also owns the land where the official operated a used car dealership.

Mark Hunt , 66, is accused of using his position as a state official to improperly transfer several tax-delinquent properties to a real estate company owned by the wife of his friend, Charleston attorney Robert Johns , despite the warnings of other state employees that such transactions violated state law.

Federal prosecutors announced on Monday that a federal grand jury had indicted Hunt, Johns, and three employees of the State Auditor’s Office in connection with the alleged scheme, alleging the group bypassed legal requirements to transfer ownership of properties located in Kanawha and Boone counties.

The charges against Hunt come on the heels of a West Virginia Watch investigation that revealed his used car dealership, After Hours Used Auto, operated on land owned by Johns' company, NAJ LLC.

The 9 property transfers that raised red flags 

At the center of the alleged scheme were nine properties in Kanawha and Boone counties whose owners were behind on their property taxes.

Under state law, tax-delinquent properties can eventually be transferred to investors who meet certain legal requirements. But prosecutors allege those requirements were ignored in this case.

A real estate company called MAPA Inc., owned by Johns' wife, Patricia Johns , attempted to purchase the properties, according to West Virginia…
items.t: West Virginia Official Accused of Stealing 9 Properties for Friend With Ties to His Used Car Dealership

items.title: Resident of Collapsed Brooklyn Building Sues for Negligence After Losing $100K Record Collection
items.summary:
The first of what is likely to be several lawsuits was filed in Kings County Superior Court on Monday, alleging widespread negligence by a host of landlords, construction companies, and contractors in last week's deadly Brooklyn building collapse .

Dengane Omari Jack lived at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which collapsed last Wednesday, tragically killing eight people and wounding 18 more. Jack was at work at the time of the collapse, but he rushed home to see if his extensive reggae vinyl record collection, valued at $100,000, might be salvaged. It was a total loss.

"He was one of the lucky ones," a friend wrote on a GoFundMe campaign to support Jack. "But surviving came at an unimaginable cost: in a matter of seconds, he lost his home, everything he owned, and a lifetime's worth of memories and work."

Now, Jack is suing his landlord and management company, as well as a half-dozen companies affiliated with 2625 Bedford Ave. , the lot adjacent to his Flatbush building. None of those entities has filed a response to the complaint yet in court.

The suit alleges the building's owner, Isolag Realty Group, and the property manager, Olufemi Falade , failed to take action after he pointed out cracks in the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. earlier this year.

According to the lawsuit: “During October 2026, Plaintiff observed cracks at or near the Building's entrance, photographed those cracks, and reported the condition to the landlord or management responsible for the Building.” 

The suit goes on to allege that Falade “personally received or responded to the report of the cracks on behalf…
items.t: Resident of Collapsed Brooklyn Building Sues for Negligence After Losing $100K Record Collection

items.title: Florida Homes Are Flooding in the Dry Season—and Too Many Owners Are Unprepared
items.summary:
The Sunshine State is facing an unusual bout of heavy rain and flooding in the middle of its dry season, which usually begins in November. 

The unexpected weather has put pressure on drainage systems and left standing water in many communities, particularly those in South Florida’s Broward County and along Central Florida’s Atlantic Coast in places like Daytona Beach and Cape Canaveral .

On Nov. 18, the western part of Broward County faced what meteorologists refer to as a “rain bomb.” In just 24 hours, West Hollywood received over 15 inches of rain , while surrounding neighborhoods saw about 10 inches. 

Due to the severity of the situation, which has led to issues such as stranded cars and out-of-service traffic signals, Broward County and Hollywood declared states of emergency , with Hollywood officials encouraging residents to shelter in place and avoid unnecessary travel . 

Forecasters expect additional rainfall through the end of this week as well as 2 to 4 inches across Eastern Florida, with about 4 to 8 inches from Miami to Jacksonville between Tuesday and Friday. Some areas may even get hit with up to 12 inches.

While the wet and windy conditions are expected to improve, the Southeast may see a cooler, rainier Thanksgiving this year . The rain could linger from the upper coast of Texas toward the southern Atlantic Coast throughout the holiday weekend.

“The dry season doesn’t mean your house is in the clear. Florida is currently showing us that heavy rain can flood homes miles from the beach,” says John Espenschied , owner at InsuranceBrokers.com in O'Fallon,…
items.t: Florida Homes Are Flooding in the Dry Season—and Too Many Owners Are Unprepared

items.title: In Portland, OR, Entry-Level Buyers Suddenly Have More Options
items.summary:
A new metro-by-metro analysis from Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home . These options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates create challenges for many would-be buyers.

According to research, the national share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from about $260,000 to $340,000. 

However, some cities are bucking this trend, and Portland, OR , has seen an encouraging uptick in starter homes in recent years.

Portland sees a rise in starter homes 

A starter home is defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, capturing the relative affordability of an area's lower-end market. These homes are typically smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the local median.

In the Portland-Vancouver, OR-WA , metro area, the share of starter homes has shown positive growth. The share was 28.0% in 2019 and dipped slightly to 27.8% in 2022 before rising to 32.0% in 2026. 

This represents a total increase of +4.0 percentage points since 2019, signaling growing opportunity for buyers in the market.

Renting may be the better option now 

For those deciding between renting or buying , current data suggests renting is the more affordable path for now. A July Rent Report found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This financial advantage to…
items.t: In Portland, OR, Entry-Level Buyers Suddenly Have More Options

items.title: Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month
items.summary:
Leaders at the Federal Reserve held firm on interest rates in October, but also thought a future rate hike "would likely be appropriate" as some mulled a larger hike in December, according to meeting minutes released on Wednesday.

At the Oct. 27–28 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its previous 3.75%-4.00% range. The decision came days before the 2026 midterms, even as FOMC members agreed inflation was a persistent concern.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh joined the majority, while Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both voted in favor of a quarter-point increase. One month before, the FOMC voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to clamp down on inflation. 

The minutes—which don't name FOMC members specifically while discussing their deliberations—show that some of the FOMC members considered that, while the impact of tariffs on the economy was waning, high energy costs continue to pressure Americans. 

Indeed, some participants even noted that, if the inflation numbers got too unfavorable, they would consider a rate hike of more than a quarter-percent in December. Bond markets still view that as unlikely, with the probability of a larger half-point hike next month at just 5%, according to CME FedWatch .

Still, Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller told CNBC on Wednesday it may be necessary to "shock people" with a larger rate hike. He said in a speech this month that a half-percent point hike might be necessary next month.

items.t: Fed Officials Expect Further Interest Rate Hikes After Pausing Last Month

items.title: The Thanksgiving Hosting Stress Test: Is Your Place Ready for the Big Day?
items.summary:
Hosting Thanksgiving in your first home is exciting, but it can also feel overwhelming. 

“You likely want everything to look and feel ‘put together’ as soon as possible despite the fact that a fresh move-in is typically anything but,” says Kate Pechinka , founder and principal designer of Kate Kelly Interiors in Chester Springs, PA .

The pressures of living up to the warm environment you’ve either experienced growing up or seen in movies or advertisements combined with the added demands on your home’s systems don’t make things any easier. 

“Suddenly, multiple people are using the bathrooms, the dishwasher and garbage disposal are running frequently, the oven is working for hours, and guests are moving through spaces that may not have been arranged for entertaining,” explains Kevin Vander Hyde , vice president of Vander Hyde Services in Grand Rapids, MI .

Here’s the good news: With a little preparation and planning, you can ensure your home is Thanksgiving-ready and alleviate a great deal of stress long before your guests arrive.

10 essential pre-holiday checks to make 

These expert tips can help you address safety concerns, secure your belongings, and prevent common hosting mishaps this Turkey Day—all while keeping your sanity and budget in check as a new homeowner.

1. Protect valuables 

Ensure keepsakes, special family heirlooms, and other high-value items are either put away, well protected, or displayed in a place that invites appreciation, but not direct interaction like a high mantel or glass-front china cabinet.

items.t: The Thanksgiving Hosting Stress Test: Is Your Place Ready for the Big Day?

In May 2026, the government overhauled private renting by abolishing no-fault evictions and shifting private tenancies to rolling contracts. However, deposit protection remains an issue for many private renters.

The government has promised and begun consulting on reforms, including scrapping insured deposit schemes, but has yet to confirm when this will happen. Landlords and letting agents are currently permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts and this creates a “power imbalance”, housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook has said.

items.t: Private renters in England: have you struggled to get your deposit back?

items.title: Pending Home Sales Tumble to New Record Low as High Mortgage Rates Freeze Buyers
items.summary:
Pending home sales descended to a new all-time low in October as mortgage rates surged to a three-year peak , keeping would-be buyers firmly on the sidelines.

Contract signings fell 4.7% compared to September, and plummeted 16.7% year over year, according to the National Association of Realtors® Pending Home Sales report released on Wednesday.

"October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out," says NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun . 

The October readout comes on the heels of the previous record low set in September , when pending sales fell 7.3% month over month and 11.3% year over year.

"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," says Yun. 

Same as in September, pending sales were down both month over month and year over year in all four U.S. regions. The West saw the largest monthly pullback with a 6.9% drop, followed by the South (-6.3%), Midwest (-2.7%), and Northeast (-0.8%).

Annually, the West was again at the forefront with a 20.3% drop, followed by the South (-18.7%), Midwest (-14%), and Northeast (-11.1%).

"Even though all four regions saw dramatic cooling, the relative strength of the Midwest and Northeast are clear, due largely to still-scarce inventory conditions," says Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones .

At the metro level, pending sales fell year over year even in the hitherto most resilient markets. Across the 50 largest…
items.t: Pending Home Sales Tumble to New Record Low as High Mortgage Rates Freeze Buyers

items.title: Mortgage Demand Falls 2.3% as Rates Resume Climbing After 4 Weeks of Declines
items.summary:
Mortgage applications fell last week, as interest rates rose to their highest levels in three weeks amid inflation concerns, unease over war in the Middle East, and federal rate hike expectations. 

For the week ending Nov. 13 the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index —a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—decreased 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, decreased 3% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances jumped to 7.31% this week, an increase from last week's rate of 7.21%, according to MBA calculations.

A separate survey from Freddie Mac showed mortgage rates dropped to 7.11% last week from 7.18% the week before, although new data on Thursday is expected to show an uptick.

“Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist, Joel Kan , CMB.

“Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, as renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines," Kan continued. 

In recent weeks, high interest rates had pushed more buyers toward riskier adjustable rate mortgages. However, this past week, ARM applications decreased to…
items.t: Mortgage Demand Falls 2.3% as Rates Resume Climbing After 4 Weeks of Declines

items.title: Single-Family Construction Rebounds in November, but Permits Nosedive
items.summary:
Construction of new single-family homes rose a bit in October, but permits fell sharply, the U.S. Census Bureau reported Wednesday.

Single-family housing starts rose 4% last month from September, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 864,000. On an annual basis, single-family starts were down 3.2% from a year earlier.

The monthly increase comes from upticks in the West and South, while the Northeast saw a larger increase in starts and the Midwest a slight decline. Single-family starts rose 15.7% on the month in Northeast, 4.2% in the South, and 3.4% in the West, but fell 0.8% in the Midwest.

Total privately owned housing starts, including more volatile multifamily units, rose 9.9% from September and 2.8% from October 2025. The month extends the uneven year for housing starts, which after a brief August rebound , then fell sharply in September .

Meanwhile, new building permits in October fell 7.4% month over month and 8.7% year over year to an annualized 1,295,000 units.

At the same time, housing completions increased 6.5% from September but fell 10.4% compared to last year.

Even so, the slowdown of building permits reflects greater pessimism in the housing market for builders. Many of the nation's major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue.

"The challenges facing builders have not subsided, and while there are some glimmers of hope in the housing starts figures, it must be noted that the current pace of single family home starts is still below last year’s actual total," Realtor.com® economist Joel Berner says. "This month’s data is…
items.t: Single-Family Construction Rebounds in November, But Permits Nosedive

items.title: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million
items.summary:
Angela Huffman , a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH , and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH , sheep farm.

On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky.

The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town.

"We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com® . Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant.

"What does that do to the community?" she says.

Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures.

Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone. 

Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment…
items.t: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million

items.title: Rents Rise Annually for First Time in 3 Years as Multifamily Building Boom Stalls
items.summary:
The median asking rent posted its first annual increase in more than three years in October, fueled by a sharp nationwide pullback in multifamily construction.

October marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly rental report . The increase was modest, with the median asking rent rising by just $1 to $1,692, but the underlying data suggests more hikes could follow. 

Larger units drove the rebound. Two-bedrooms led the way, with median asking rent rising 0.3% year over year to $1,889, followed by one-bedrooms, which edged up 0.1% to $1,566. 

Meanwhile, studio rents continued to lag, falling 1.2% from October 2025 to $1,411.

"I see this as the market beginning to rebalance,"  Lissette Calderon , CEO of Neology Group , a Miami-based real estate development firm, tells Realtor.com. "We had an extraordinary amount of new supply delivered over the last few years, and it takes time for that inventory to be absorbed. With construction slowing and demand for rental housing remaining strong, I expect rent growth to gradually return, particularly in markets where employment and household growth continue to support housing demand." 

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu confirms that last month's rent turnaround hinges on a shifting supply pipeline.

The post-pandemic multifamily construction boom of 2021–22 flooded the market with fresh rental units completed in 2023–25, keeping prices in check.

Now, a broad cooling in multifamily construction is easing downward pressure on rent, just as high mortgage rates…
items.t: Rents Rise Annually for First Time in 3 Years as Multifamily Building Boom Stalls

items.title: Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009
items.summary:
As economic pressures continue to rise, a shocking new study has found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership has fallen 46% since 2009.

TransUnion, a leader in global information and insights, released its 2027 Personal and Commercial Lines Annual Insurance Outlook on Tuesday, which focuses on what the insurance industry needs to stay profitable in a changing market.

The report states that personal line underwriting has been strong throughout this year, but companies need to assess their strategies going forward as fewer people buy cars and homes , therefore reducing the pool of potential policyholders.

According to the report, the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a sharp decline from 7.2% in 2009.

This represents a shocking 46% decrease in the share of renters transitioning to homeownership in just 14 years.

Combined with a 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors®, which stated that the median age of first-time buyers climbed from 33 to 40 in just five years, TransUnion concluded that the pool of potential policyholders is shrinking.

The decrease in renters buying homes goes back to affordability and economic pressure, according to Ryan Thomson of The Assumable Guy .

“Renters didn't stop wanting to own. Rates tripled and prices kept climbing, so the monthly number stopped working,” Thomson tells Realtor.com® . “In Colorado Springs, where I sell, 71% of households could afford a median-priced home in 2019. By 2023, it was 25.3%. So renters stay put. Or they move wherever the payment still works.”…
items.t: Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009

items.title: Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home
items.summary:
Daniel Craig first stepped into the role of James Bond 20 years ago, and now, he has officially passed the duties along to someone new: Robert Pattinson .

Craig made his 007 debut in the 2006 film “Casino Royale” and held the legendary gig for 15 years. He had originally planned to play the British spy for four films, but ended up having a successful five-movie run with “Quantum Solace” (2008), “Skyfall” (2012), “Spectre” (2015), and “No Time To Die” (2021).

In addition to filming one more motion picture than he had planned, Craig, 58, has spoken out about how physically demanding it is to be James Bond. In the time between the last two films, he told The Sunday Times he was “getting old.”

“I’m creaky,” he admitted in the 2019 interview. In 2024, he told The New York Times , “I find it really hard, this job, and it gets harder as I get older.”

Beyond the grueling stunts and action required for each installment, the role demanded a huge time commitment that pulled Craig away from his family.

Daniel Craig's reign as James Bond ended with the 2021 film "No Time to Die." It was recently announced Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role. (Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Omega) 

Craig played 007 for 15 years, an experience he said was "really hard." (PIERRE-PHILIPPE MARCOU/AFP/GettyImages) 

Toward the end of his run, Craig joked that he was getting "creaky" and was no longer up to the intense stunts and physicality required of the role. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images)

items.t: Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home

items.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
items.summary:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.

items.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.
